title: AND, OR, NOT, XOR and implication as linear constraints

questions.stem: An analyst writes the rule "project A needs project B" as the row x_A >= x_B. Which plans does that model get wrong?

options.text: It allows A without B, and refuses B without A
options.says: Right: x_A >= x_B says "if B then A", so it refuses 01 and allows 10, the reverse of the rule.

options.text: It allows B without A, and refuses A without B
options.says: That is what the correct row x_A <= x_B does, and it is what the rule asks for.

options.text: It allows A and B together, and refuses each one alone
options.says: Refusing each one alone is x_A = x_B; x_A >= x_B allows A alone.

options.text: It allows every plan, since a reversed row is never enforced
options.says: A reversed row is a valid row and the solver enforces it; it enforces a different rule.

origin.section: AND or OR on Either Side of an Implication Is Still One Row

questions.stem: Rule: if both the reservoir R and the pump station S are funded, the telemetry project T must be funded too; R or S alone asks nothing of T. Which row states the rule?

options.says: With R and S both funded the left side is 2, so this row refuses every plan that funds both.
Right: the left side is 1 only when both are funded, and 0 or -1 otherwise.
This is "if R or S then T": R alone already forces x_T up to at least 0.5, so to 1.
These two rows say "if R or S then T", which asks T of R alone.

origin.section: AND or OR on Either Side of an Implication Is Still One Row

questions.stem: A model adds $80k of value for every county that gets a new tower. The binary y_c means county c gets one, and the only rows on it are y_c >= x_i for each tower i in county c. What can go wrong?

options.text: Nothing, since these rows tie each y_c to the towers in its county
options.says: They tie y_c in one direction only: they push it up when a tower is built and never push it down.

options.text: The solver can set y_c to 0 where a tower is built, losing value
options.says: y_c >= x_i forbids exactly that, and the reward makes the solver want y_c at 1 anyway.

options.text: The solver can set y_c to 1 where no tower is built, claiming value
options.says: Right: the reward pushes y_c up and no row pushes it down, as the region credit did with the up rows only.

options.text: The model becomes infeasible, since no y_c can satisfy every row
options.says: y_c = 1 satisfies every row y_c >= x_i, so the rows never conflict.

origin.section: Pin Only the Side the Model Would Exploit, or Both When Unsure
